lead: After this unit you can explain why a laser needs population inversion, calculate photon energy and fibre numerical aperture, and describe a fibre-optic link from source to detector. You can also compare ruby, He-Ne, Nd:YAG, CO2, dye and semiconductor lasers by medium, wavelength and use.
about: This unit explains how lasers produce coherent light and how optical fibres guide it. Chapter 5.1 starts with spontaneous and stimulated emission and Einstein's coefficients. Chapter 5.2 adds population inversion, pumping and laser characteristics. Chapters 5.3 and 5.4 describe common solid, gas and dye lasers; 5.5 covers the semiconductor laser; 5.6 lists applications. The fibre half begins at 5.7 with total internal reflection, core and cladding. Chapter 5.8 compares step-index, graded-index, single-mode and multimode fibres. Chapter 5.9 treats attenuation, the communication link and fibre sensors. Each chapter uses one worked numerical example so the formulas are tied to measured values.

chapters.idea: Atoms emit light by spontaneous or stimulated emission; Einstein's A and B coefficients compare the three rates.
chapters.depth: Define absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission with photon in and out pictures. Write the rate equation dN2/dt = −A21N2 − B21N2u(ν) + B12N1u(ν); define N1 and N2 as atoms per cubic metre, u(ν) as energy density per unit frequency in J m⁻³ Hz⁻¹, A21 in s⁻¹, and B12 and B21 as the Einstein coefficients. State B12 = B21 for non-degenerate levels and A21/B21 = 8πhν³/c³; h is Planck constant, ν frequency, c speed of light. Mention that a stimulated photon is in phase and in the same direction. Keep the Planck relation to one line.
chapters.figure: blocks: absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission with incoming and outgoing photon arrows.
chapters.example: A laser pulse carries 1.0 mJ at λ = 632.8 nm. Find the photon energy in joules and eV and the number of photons. Use h = 6.626×10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00×10⁸ m/s. E = hc/λ = 3.14×10⁻¹⁹ J = 1.96 eV; N = 1.0×10⁻³ / 3.14×10⁻¹⁹ = 3.2×10¹⁵ photons.
chapters.trap: Do not treat spontaneous emission as stimulated; the A/B relation changes strongly with ν because of the ν³ factor.
chapters.prereq: Unit 6: photon energy and photoelectric effect; Unit 3: electromagnetic waves.
chapters.leave: Population inversion and laser cavity to 5.2; specific lasers to 5.3–5.5.

chapters.idea: Laser action needs more atoms in the upper level than the lower level, maintained by pumping, inside an optical cavity.
chapters.depth: Define population inversion as N2 > N1, a metastable level, and pumping by optical, electrical or chemical means. Compare three-level and four-level schemes. State the threshold condition: gain must exceed losses in one round trip. List laser characteristics: monochromaticity with small Δλ, coherence, directionality with small divergence, and high brightness. Define the resonator with two mirrors and a gain medium. Mention continuous and pulsed operation. No detailed rate equations beyond the threshold idea.
chapters.figure: blocks: pump source drives gain medium to inversion; two mirrors feed light back; output beam leaves one mirror.
chapters.example: For a transition of energy 1.96 eV at T = 300 K, find the thermal-equilibrium ratio N2/N1. Compare it with an inverted ratio N2/N1 = 2. Use k = 8.617×10⁻⁵ eV/K. kT = 0.02585 eV; N2/N1 = exp(−1.96/0.02585) ≈ 1.2×10⁻³³, far below 2, so pumping is needed.
chapters.trap: A larger pump does not guarantee inversion; threshold and non-radiative losses matter, and three-level lasers need more than half the atoms pumped.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 Einstein coefficients; Unit 6: Boltzmann factor is useful.
chapters.leave: Construction details of named lasers to 5.3–5.5; applications to 5.6.

chapters.idea: Ruby is a pulsed three-level solid-state laser; He-Ne is a continuous gas laser that transfers energy from helium to neon.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this; keep it short. Ruby: Cr³⁺ ions in Al₂O₃, flashlamp pump, three-level scheme, output 694.3 nm, pulsed. He-Ne: He-Ne gas mixture in a discharge tube, He metastable state transfers energy to Ne, four-level action, output 632.8 nm, continuous. Draw simplified energy levels only; skip cavity design and gas-discharge equations.
chapters.figure: blocks: ruby three-level cycle and He-Ne energy transfer side by side; mark pump, metastable level and output.
chapters.example: A ruby laser gives a 1.0 J pulse at 694.3 nm. Find the number of photons in the pulse. E = hc/λ = 2.86×10⁻¹⁹ J; N = 1.0 / 2.86×10⁻¹⁹ = 3.5×10¹⁸ photons.
chapters.trap: Ruby is three-level and pulsed, not four-level continuous; He-Ne output is 632.8 nm, not the ruby red line at 694.3 nm.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 population inversion and pumping; 5.1 photon energy.
chapters.leave: Nd:YAG, CO2 and dye to 5.4; semiconductor to 5.5.

chapters.idea: Nd:YAG, CO2 and dye lasers show how the gain medium sets wavelength, power and tuning range.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this; keep it short. Nd:YAG: Nd³⁺ in YAG crystal, four-level, optical pump, 1064 nm, pulsed or continuous. CO2: CO2-N2-He gas mixture, electrical discharge, 10.6 μm, high power for cutting and welding. Dye: organic dye solution, broad visible band, tunable by grating, optical pump. Compare medium, wavelength, pump and typical use in a small table.
chapters.figure: array: comparison rows for Nd:YAG, CO2 and dye lasers with medium, wavelength, pump and use.
chapters.example: A CO2 laser emits at λ = 10.6 μm. Find the photon energy in joules and eV and the frequency. E = hc/λ = 1.87×10⁻²⁰ J = 0.117 eV; ν = c/λ = 2.83×10¹³ Hz.
chapters.trap: CO2 laser wavelength is 10.6 μm, not 10.6 nm; Nd:YAG is 1064 nm, not 1064 μm.

chapters.idea: A forward-biased semiconductor p-n junction can invert carriers and emit laser light from a tiny cleaved cavity.
chapters.depth: Explain direct band gap, active region, forward bias injecting electrons and holes, recombination, population inversion, and cleaved facets as mirrors. Mention homojunction and double heterostructure and threshold current. Define band gap Eg and the relation λ ≈ hc/Eg. Compare with an LED: an LED has no cavity and no threshold. Keep material details to the GaAs example.
chapters.figure: blocks: forward bias injects carriers into active region; recombination emits photons; cleaved facets reflect light; beam exits.
chapters.example: A GaAs semiconductor laser has band gap Eg = 1.42 eV. Find the emission wavelength. Use hc = 1240 eV nm. λ = 1240 / 1.42 = 873 nm.
chapters.trap: Silicon has an indirect band gap and is a poor light emitter; an LED is not a laser because it lacks feedback and a threshold.
chapters.prereq: Unit 7: p-n junction and energy bands; 5.2 inversion.
chapters.leave: Laser applications to 5.6; fibre coupling to 5.9.

chapters.idea: Lasers are chosen for applications by wavelength, power, coherence and pulse length.
chapters.depth: Cover categories: material processing such as cutting, welding and drilling; medicine such as ophthalmic surgery and dermatology; communication as the source for fibre links; measurement with rangefinders, interferometers and LIDAR; data storage and printing with CD, DVD, Blu-ray and barcode scanning; holography and spectroscopy. Give one Indian everyday example such as barcode scanning at a shop or a laser source in a fibre broadband link. No detailed surgical procedures.
chapters.figure: tree: laser applications split into industry, medicine, communication, measurement and consumer uses.
chapters.example: A laser rangefinder sends a pulse and receives the echo after 20.0 ns. Find the distance to the target. d = ct/2 = (3.00×10⁸ × 20.0×10⁻⁹) / 2 = 3.0 m.
chapters.trap: The echo travels to the target and back, so forgetting the factor 1/2 doubles the distance.
chapters.prereq: 5.3–5.5 laser types; Unit 4: interference for measurement uses.
chapters.leave: Fibre communication details to 5.9; holography theory to Unit 4 if taught.

chapters.idea: An optical fibre guides light by total internal reflection in a core with higher refractive index than its cladding.
chapters.depth: Define core, cladding, buffer and jacket. State total internal reflection and critical angle θc = sin⁻¹(n2/n1) with n1 > n2. Define numerical aperture NA = √(n1² − n2²) and acceptance angle θa = sin⁻¹(NA) in air. Explain the meridional ray picture. Mention that NA measures light-gathering power. Keep the derivation short.
chapters.figure: stack: fibre layers from centre out — core, cladding, buffer, jacket.
chapters.example: A fibre has n1 = 1.50 and n2 = 1.48. Find the critical angle, numerical aperture and acceptance angle in air. θc = sin⁻¹(1.48/1.50) = 80.6°; NA = √(1.50² − 1.48²) = 0.244; θa = sin⁻¹(0.244) = 14.1°.
chapters.trap: Use n2/n1 for the critical angle, not n1/n2; NA uses the square root of the difference of squares.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4: refraction and total internal reflection; Unit 3: EM waves.
chapters.leave: Fibre types to 5.8; attenuation and links to 5.9.

chapters.idea: The refractive-index profile and core size decide whether a fibre is step or graded, single or multimode.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this; keep it short. Step-index: abrupt n change; multimode step-index has modal dispersion. Graded-index: n falls smoothly from centre, rays curve, less modal dispersion. Single-mode: small core, one propagation mode, high bandwidth; multimode: large core, many modes. Define V = (2πa/λ)√(n1²−n2²) with a as core radius; single mode when V < 2.405. Mention approximate mode count M ≈ V²/2 for step-index multimode. No full waveguide mathematics.
chapters.figure: plot: refractive index against radius for step-index and graded-index profiles, with single-mode and multimode core sizes noted.
chapters.example: A step-index fibre has core diameter 50 μm, n1 = 1.48, n2 = 1.46 and λ = 1.30 μm. Find V and the approximate number of modes. a = 25 μm; NA = √(1.48² − 1.46²) = 0.2425; V = (2π×25/1.30)×0.2425 = 29.3; M ≈ V²/2 = 429.
chapters.trap: Use core radius, not diameter, in V; V < 2.405 means single mode, not many modes.

chapters.idea: Attenuation sets the repeater spacing in a fibre link, while fibre sensors turn changes in light into measurements.
chapters.depth: Define attenuation α in dB/km: α = (10/L) log10(Pin/Pout), with L in km. List absorption, Rayleigh scattering and bending losses. Draw a fibre-optic communication link: encoder and driver, source such as LED or laser, fibre, photodetector, amplifier and receiver, repeater. Define a fibre sensor as one that uses intensity, phase or wavelength changes caused by temperature, strain, pressure or rotation. Mention advantages such as immunity to electrical interference. Keep sensor types to examples.
chapters.figure: blocks: transmitter with laser or LED → optical fibre → photodetector → receiver; add repeater and a sensor branch.
chapters.example: A 2.0 km fibre has input power 1.0 mW and output power 0.50 mW. Find the attenuation in dB/km. Loss = 10 log10(1.0/0.50) = 3.01 dB; α = 3.01/2.0 = 1.5 dB/km.
chapters.trap: Attenuation uses log10, not ln; the answer is per km, so divide total dB by length.
chapters.prereq: 5.7 fibre structure; 5.8 modes and bandwidth; 5.5 semiconductor laser as source.
chapters.leave: Detailed optical receiver design to electronics; sensor signal processing to instrumentation.
